questions.prompt: Which command stages every changed file for the next commit?
explanations: git push uploads commits to GitHub. It doesn't stage anything.
Correct: git add . stages every change in the current folder.
git commit saves what is already staged. Staging comes first, with git add.
git init creates a new repository. You only run it once per project.
questions.hint: Staging means choosing what goes into the next snapshot.

questions.prompt: You edited index.html and ran git commit -m "Update header". Git replies "nothing added to commit". What went wrong?
options: The commit message is too short
You didn't stage the change with git add
index.html is not a valid file name
explanations: Git accepts short messages. The message isn't the problem.
Correct: only staged changes are committed, so run git add index.html first.
Pushing comes after committing. There is nothing to push yet.
index.html is a perfectly valid file name.
questions.hint: Which of the three areas does git commit read from?

questions.prompt: What is in the staging area?
options: Every file in your project folder
Changes you have chosen to include in the next commit
Commits that are waiting on GitHub
explanations: That's the working directory. Staging only holds the changes you picked with git add.
Correct: the staging area is the next commit being prepared.
GitHub holds pushed commits. The staging area is on your computer, before any commit.
Ignored files never enter the staging area.
questions.hint: Think of it as the box you pack before sealing a snapshot.

questions.prompt: Which commit message is most useful?
explanations: Fix what? In a long history this tells you nothing.
Correct: specific and written as an instruction.
Random letters make the history impossible to search.
Numbered vague messages don't say what changed.
questions.hint: Good messages say what changed, as a short instruction.

explanations: Two commits can have the same message.
Correct: every commit gets a unique hash. The verifier records it as proof of your work.
Two people can commit at the same moment.
Many commits change the same files.
questions.hint: The projector shows it next to every verified quest.

options: Saves a snapshot on your computer
Sends your commits to the remote repository on GitHub
Downloads the latest commits from GitHub
explanations: That's git commit.
Correct: push uploads commits to origin, usually GitHub.
That's git pull.
That's git add.
questions.hint: Push sends up, pull brings down.

questions.prompt: You pushed your work, but the workshop verifier says "Repository not found". What's the most likely cause?
options: You used git add . instead of git add index.html
explanations: Correct: the verifier can only read public repositories. Change the visibility in the repository settings.
Both forms stage files. This doesn't affect whether the repository can be found.
Spaces in messages are normal.
The number of files doesn't hide a repository.
questions.hint: Who is allowed to see the repository?

questions.prompt: Put these commands in order to publish a brand-new project (the GitHub remote is already added).
explanations: Create the repository (init), stage the files (add), save the snapshot (commit), then upload it (push).

questions.prompt: Which line makes a heading in Markdown?
explanations: Double asterisks make bold text.
Correct: # starts a heading; ## makes a smaller one.
A dash starts a bullet-list item.
Angle brackets aren't Markdown syntax for headings.
questions.hint: It's a single symbol at the start of the line.

questions.prompt: Spot the bug in this README. Which line is broken?
questions.code:
1  # Ana's Portfolio
2  Built during the GenAI web workshop.
3  [Live site](https://ana.github.io
4  - HTML, CSS and Three.js
explanations: A # heading with an apostrophe is fine.
A plain sentence becomes a paragraph. Nothing wrong here.
Correct: the link is missing its closing bracket. It should end with ...github.io)
A dash makes a valid list item.
questions.hint: Links look like [text](address). Count the brackets.

questions.prompt: Which prompt will get you the most useful answer?
options: You are a patient Git teacher. I'm on Windows with a folder called portfolio. Give me numbered steps to create a repo, add a README and push it to https://github.com/ana/portfolio, and explain each command.
Do everything for my GitHub, quickly
explanations: Too vague: the AI has to guess what you want.
Which commands? For what? Missing task, context and format.
Correct: role, task, context, constraints and output format are all there.
"Everything" and "quickly" give the AI nothing specific to work with.
questions.hint: Role, task, context, constraints, output format.

questions.prompt: The AI suggests a command you don't understand. What should you do?
options: Ask the AI to explain it line by line first
explanations: Some commands delete or overwrite work. Understand first.
Correct: you stay in control and you learn something.
No need to give up. Ask for an explanation instead.
That doesn't help you understand or run it safely.
questions.hint: You are the pilot; the AI is the co-pilot.
